name: Ads in AI: Four Placements, One Label
question: How does a paid product end up inside an AI assistant's answer?
problem: You ask an AI assistant which laptop to buy and it names one. A sponsored product can get into that answer four ways, and a "Sponsored" label only works on one of them.
points: Know the four placements: a slot under the answer, an item in the list, a retrieved page, a line in the system prompt. Only the slot leaves the answer unchanged.
Building an assistant: write down what the model is never paid to say, and run a replay with the sponsor removed, before the ad slot exists.
Using one: ask two assistants the same question. It isn't proof, but it's the check on your side.

code.what: A one-page template: which placements are open, what the model is never paid to say, and the replay that checks it.

stands_on.why: the same mechanism, with a commercial payload and the operator as the injector

title: How a Product Gets Into an AI Assistant's Answer — Four Placements, One Label #shorts
cover_title: ADS IN AI — PRODUCT TRACK · PART ONE
cover_title_alt: A LABEL WORKS ON A SLOT. NOT ON A SENTENCE.
caption:
Ads in AI assistants — where they actually go, and why the "Sponsored" label doesn't work in a chat.
AI Product · Part 14 · first of three. Stands on Part 11 (prompt injection).

You ask an AI assistant which laptop to buy. It names one. How did that laptop get in there? Four placements. The sponsored label covers exactly one.

In search, an ad is a slot — top of the page, visual label on it. Half of people still miss the label. An AI response has none. But a slot is a thing: move it, remove it, don't click it. A label works on a slot, not on a sentence.

Four placements for sponsored content in an AI chatbot answer:
① a slot under the answer — separate system, the model never sees it
② the list — the sponsored product sits inside the recommendations
③ the retrieved page
④ the system prompt — the operator's words, not yours

Every placement except the separate slot changes the answer. One line in the system prompt — a suggestion, not an order — and 18 of 23 models picked the sponsored product more than half the time, at twice the price. Same mechanism as prompt injection; this time the operator is the one injecting.

The label: in a preregistered experiment (2,012 people, real catalogue), a sponsored recommendation inside a chat won 61%. Add the word "Sponsored" — still 55%. A sponsored slot in search: 22%. The label did six points of work. The sentence did thirty-nine.

Can you tell? Under 10% when the model is told to be subtle. Half of people miss an ad even when it's disclosed. And no advertising regulator — India, US, EU — has a rule for an ad that isn't a discrete unit.

One check works. Same question, sponsor removed. Different answer? That's the placement.

Building an AI assistant? That diff is a written list of what the model is never paid to say, plus a replay that runs it — before the ad slot exists.
Using one? Ask twice — two assistants, same question. Not proof, but the only check on your side.

experiment.variable: track: first of three consecutive AI Product parts; structure, hook shape and runtime band held at Part 13 settings. Follow ask moved back to the end card (Part 13's mid-roll ask got 0 follows) — a second variable, acknowledged
experiment.hypothesis: a product part holds the engineering audience — retention and follow rate at or above the engineering baseline — so the page can carry two tracks without losing the first
experiment.metric: retention_pct (avg_watch_time_s / runtime_s) and follows_per_1000_viewers; day-7 views as the category check
experiment.baseline: retention 20% (Parts 12, 13); follows/1,000 ~7–9 (Parts 11–12; Part 13: 0); day-7 views ~1,700 typical (Part 13: 398)
experiment.win: trio average retention >=25% AND follows/1,000 >=9; per-part read at day 7, decision on the trio
experiment.notes: Supersedes the planned E2 (reply CTA) in Claude outputs/reel-experiments.md; that variable is parked. Lose → product parts alternate with engineering instead of running consecutive, and the name field stays 'AI Engineering'. Win → name field becomes 'AI Engineering & Product' after part 16 and a PRODUCT highlight is created. Category check: if this part lands below Part 13 on views AND follows, the topic is the problem, not the track. Follows/1,000 is read knowing the CTA position also changed vs Part 13; compare against Parts 11–12 (end-card asks) for that metric. Guards: same gates as engineering parts; every product part names the engineering part it stands on (this one: Part 11).
